coherence.reasons: Both documents carry the same governing thought (fix gross margin and delivery economics, not headcount; firm levers reach ~2.6%, a second wave closes to 3.0%) and the same diagnosis-options-plan-first moves flow. Y's executive summary is a cleaner hierarchy: four top-level claims, each with two supporting lines, and each claim reappears as a section lead. X's summary has claims sitting under the wrong heading (the draft-plan verdict under DIAGNOSIS, the covenant claim under PLAN), and its slide 4 inserts a test of the team's own hypothesis before the diagnosis has been shown, so it cites results from later pages. Y also gives one message per slide where X packs several (promotion economics versus ValuMart defence; per-order loss versus the 6.1% reconciliation), and adds a slide supporting the targeted-labour lever, which is the one lever that sits awkwardly with 'not headcount'. Against Y: its 'Executive summary' and 'Next steps' titles carry no message, and the section-divider slides add no content. The difference is small because the underlying logic is the same.

judgment.reasons: The recommendation is identical: reject the 8% cut and the freeze, adopt a sized margin-first plan (promotion pruning, vendor funding, private label, shrink, targeted labour, delivery repricing, six store exits), hold a second wave and a click-and-collect-only fallback that needs the owners' consent. Both weigh the same alternatives and the same four trade-offs (labour versus shrink, promotions versus ValuMart traffic, delivery versus the owners' wish, store exits versus exit cost and board vote). Both are honest that the firm levers reach only ~2.6% and that about half of the second wave is needed. Y is slightly stronger on the one conditional element, the 3% labour-hours reduction: its slide 17 says the hours come out of Q3/Q4 stores where shrink barely responds, that receiving and produce rotation are protected everywhere, that ~78,000 hours go back into lean stores, and that a pilot tests the correlation first. X makes the same points but scattered across the lever table, slide 8 and the roadmap. Y also states that the store notices add nothing in FY2026, which makes the covenant case clearer.

evidence.reasons: The numbers are essentially the same and match the answer key in both: margin 3.37% to 1.02%; bridge of e-commerce −$12.6M, promotions −$10.5M, shrink −$7.5M, labour −$4.5M (13%), occupancy −$3.0M, private label +$2.7M; e-commerce drag −$10.4M; the 6.1% claim reconciled to −$0.5M before cannibalisation; store exits $6.6M for all nine and $4.4M for six; fee test worth ~$2.5M. Both treat the category team's 'promotions work' claim as correlation and show the comp gain repays less than half its cost, and both treat the shrink-by-quartile pattern as correlation to be piloted. Both rest on the same unsupported team allowances (one-time costs, 25% lost volume, phasing, 40% switching, pro-rata store split) and both disclose them. Y is marginally more careful: it flags at the point of use that the $42.9M for option C, the $3.0M cost-recovery figure, the 2.4% checkpoint and the $1.0M private-label figure are the analysis's own estimates, not rebuilt from the pack, and it explains the $16.9M versus $17.0M rounding. X shows these as plain figures in the body and discloses them only in the appendix. Small rounding differences (shrink sensitivity $2.1M versus $2.2M, high case $38.0M versus $37.9M) are immaterial.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's 'wage inflation is the main cause' view in the same way and on the same evidence: labour is 13% of the decline, productivity absorbed two-thirds of the 9.4% wage rise, the leanest-labour quartile runs 3.1% shrink against 2.3%, and the draft plan nets to ~1.1% after $3.8–7.5M of shrink giveback. Both reject the freeze because it locks in the $10.4M loss, and both keep a targeted labour element rather than dismissing labour entirely. X places the hypothesis test and its 'revised answer' in the main body; Y moves the same table to the appendix but keeps 'starting levers are not enough' on the plan slide. That test concerns the team's own margin-first hypothesis more than the pack's, so the placement makes no meaningful difference to how management's hypothesis is handled.

overall.reasons: These are the same analysis and the same recommendation, so the decision maker reaches the same decision with either. Y serves slightly better: a cleaner summary hierarchy, one message per slide on promotions and e-commerce, a dedicated justification of the targeted-labour lever against the shrink risk, and explicit point-of-use flags on the figures that are team estimates rather than pack data. X's advantages are compactness and having the hypothesis test in the main flow; its misplaced summary headings and denser slides are minor weaknesses. The margin is small.
